points.what: Arrange data as a 2-D feature matrix X (rows are samples, columns are features) and a 1-D target y, and check their shapes before handing them to scikit-learn.
Use the estimator pattern: create a model object, call fit(X, y) to learn from data, then predict(X_new) to get predictions.
Explain how transformers learn something from data in fit, apply it in transform, and combine both with fit_transform, and why the fitted values are reused on new data.
Split X and y into training and test portions with train_test_split, and control the test size and shuffling.
Tell apart hyperparameters, which you set when creating the model, from fitted attributes ending in an underscore, which are learned by fit, and look at both with get_params and the attributes.
Set random_state so splits and randomized models give the same results on every run, and know why results can differ without it.
Rescale numeric features with StandardScaler or MinMaxScaler, fitting only on training data, and explain why distance-based and regularized models need it.
Turn categorical columns into 0/1 indicator columns with OneHotEncoder, and handle categories that appear only in new data.
Fill missing values inside a model workflow with SimpleImputer so the fill values are learned from training data only.
Apply different transformers to different columns (for example scale numbers and one-hot encode categories) with ColumnTransformer and get one combined feature matrix.
Chain preprocessing steps and a final model into a single Pipeline that is fitted and used like one estimator, and see how this prevents leakage.
Create squared and interaction features with PolynomialFeatures so a linear model can fit curved relationships, and recognise the risk of too many features.
Fit a linear regression model with LinearRegression and understand that it finds the straight line or plane that minimizes squared error.
Read coef_ and intercept_ to say how the prediction changes when a feature goes up by one unit, and know why scale affects how comparable coefficients are.
Use Ridge and Lasso to penalize large coefficients, see how the alpha hyperparameter trades fit against simplicity, and know that Lasso can set coefficients to exactly zero.
Compute MAE, MSE, RMSE and R² on predictions, explain what each one measures, and choose among them for a problem.
Fit LogisticRegression for classification and explain that it models class probabilities from a weighted sum of features, with C controlling regularization.
Classify a point by the majority class among its k closest training points, and see how k and feature scaling change the result.
Fit a DecisionTreeClassifier, read the splits it makes, and use max_depth and similar settings to control overfitting.
Use a support vector classifier to find a wide-margin boundary, and understand the roles of the kernel and C.
Get class probabilities with predict_proba and turn them into labels with a chosen threshold instead of the default 0.5.
Build a baseline with DummyClassifier (for example always predicting the most common class) and use it as the score a real model must beat.
Compute accuracy and explain why it can look high while being useless when one class is much rarer than the other.
Read a confusion matrix to count true and false positives and negatives and see which kinds of mistakes a classifier makes.
Compute precision, recall and F1 from the confusion matrix, and pick which one matters for a given cost of mistakes.
Read an ROC curve and AUC as a summary of how well a classifier ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds.
Estimate model performance more reliably by splitting the training data into folds and averaging scores with cross_val_score.
Pick a cross-validation splitter that suits the data: KFold in general, StratifiedKFold for imbalanced classes, GroupKFold when rows from one group must stay together.
Search a grid of hyperparameter values with GridSearchCV, using cross-validation, and read best_params_ and best_score_.
Sample hyperparameter combinations at random from distributions with RandomizedSearchCV to cover large search spaces at a fixed budget.
Plot learning curves and validation curves to tell whether a model suffers from high bias or high variance and whether more data or a different setting would help.
Set aside a final test set that is used once, after all tuning, and explain why repeated peeking at it makes the score too optimistic.
Train a RandomForest, which averages many decorrelated trees built on random samples and features, and understand why this reduces overfitting compared with a single tree.
Use HistGradientBoostingClassifier or Regressor, which builds trees one after another to correct earlier errors, and tune its main settings such as learning rate and number of iterations.
Rank features by impurity-based importances and by permutation importance on held-out data, and know when each one can mislead.
